ARES: Autonomous Real-Time Evaluation System
An AI-Driven Multi-Modal Truth Infrastructure for
Misinformation Defense
Gurarpit Singh
Abstract—In an era where misinformation poses a
strategic threat to public safety, democratic processes,
and global stability, traditional fact-checking and de-
tection methods fall short—lacking speed, scalability,
and contextual depth. This paper presents ARES (Au-
tonomous Real-time Evaluation System), an AI-driven,
multi-modal misinformation detection and threat in-
telligence framework. Unlike existing systems limited
to static text analysis or isolated classifiers, ARES
integrates real-time processing of text, images, audio,
video, and URLs with geopolitical inference, behavioral
analytics, and symbolic reasoning. Its architecture
features a triple-layered verification engine, deepfake
and voice tampering detection, semantic drift tracking,
and adversarial robustness, all tied into an actionable
dashboard for analysts.
Through
comprehensive
benchmarking,
ARES
demonstrates superior accuracy (F1-score: 0.92), low-
latency performance (415 ms/claim), and high resilience
under stress scenarios such as election interference and
health infodemics. Designed for deployment in national
security, disaster response, and information warfare
settings, ARES marks a paradigm shift toward scalable,
autonomous digital truth infrastructure.
Index Terms—Misinformation Detection, Fake News,
Multi-modal AI, Deepfake Detection, Threat Intelli-
gence, Digital Truth Infrastructure

I. Introduction
In the contemporary digital ecosystem, misinformation
has evolved from a societal nuisance into a national and
global security threat. False or manipulated information
now influences democratic elections, incites violence, under-
mines public health initiatives, and accelerates geopolitical
conflicts at unprecedented scale. Both state and non-state
actors increasingly weaponize disinformation to advance
political, economic, and ideological objectives, rendering
traditional countermeasures insufficient.
Let the rate of misinformation propagation be denoted
by λp, and the rate of detection by conventional systems be
λd. In existing infrastructures, empirical evidence suggests:
λd ≪λp
implying that false narratives often achieve wide dissem-
ination before corrective action can be applied.
Current mitigation strategies primarily rely on manual
fact-checking organizations, browser-based extensions, or
platform-integrated content flags. While effective in limited
contexts, these approaches are inherently reactive, narrowly
scoped, and constrained by latency. Manual verification
fails to scale with content velocity, while automated
platform flags lack transparency, multi-modality, and
geopolitical awareness. Furthermore, most existing systems
are vulnerable to adversarial manipulation and incapable
of tracking the temporal evolution of misinformation
narratives across languages, formats, and platforms.
To address these limitations, we propose ARES (Au-
tonomous Real-time Evaluation System), a next-
generation AI-driven infrastructure designed not merely as
a fake news detector, but as a comprehensive misinforma-
tion threat intelligence framework. ARES integrates:
• multi-modal content analysis across text, image, video,
audio, and URLs,
• behavioral pattern recognition,
• geopolitical contextual intelligence,
• real-time alerting and escalation mechanisms.

contextual decision function:
V : X × C × B × T →Y
where X denotes multi-modal inputs, C represents geopo-
litical and sociocultural context, B captures behavioral
propagation signals, T denotes temporal evolution, and
Y = {True, False, Uncertain}.

This research introduces the architectural design, theo-

II. Related Work
The rise of misinformation across digital ecosystems
has led to diverse detection strategies in academic and
industrial research. Existing approaches can be broadly
categorized into: (i) manual fact-checking and platform
moderation, (ii) machine learning-based textual classifiers,
and (iii) emerging multi-modal verification systems.
Let the misinformation input space be defined as:
X = {xtext, ximg, xvid, xaud, xurl}
Most prior systems operate on a strict subset Xtext ⊂X,
resulting in limited coverage of how misinformation actually
propagates.

C. Multi-Modal and Real-Time Detection Efforts
Recent works attempt to incorporate visual and audio
forensics, such as deepfake detection using FaceForensics++
and lip-sync anomaly analysis. Knowledge graphs and
claim-matching engines have also been proposed for real-
time verification.
However, these systems operate in isolation and lack
integration with:
• Behavioral propagation analytics,
• Geopolitical context modeling,
• Temporal evolution tracking.
D. Limitations of Existing Systems
Despite progress, current solutions exhibit four critical
limitations:
1) Lack of Multi-Modality: Focused primarily on
text, ignoring images, memes, audio, and video.
2) Absence of Geopolitical Awareness: No con-
textual understanding of regional conflicts or socio-
political environments.
3) Static Intelligence: Limited real-time adaptation
and retraining capabilities.
4) Weak Threat Escalation: No scoring of psycholog-
ical, societal, or geopolitical impact.
These limitations can be summarized by the incomplete
verification function:
Vexisting : Xtext →Y
instead of the required:
Vcomplete : X × Context × Behavior × Time →Y

ARES addresses these shortcomings by unifying:
• Multi-modal claim analysis,
• Behavioral propagation modeling,

In high-stakes misinformation settings, failures rarely
occur within a single modality or task. Instead, harm
emerges from:
• cross-modal inconsistencies (e.g., authentic text paired
with synthetic audio),
• coordinated propagation behavior,
• geopolitical context misinterpretation,
• delayed or opaque decision escalation.

• to outperform the best specialized deepfake detector
on curated forensic benchmarks,

signed for full social graph access,

judgment,
• to supersede expert human fact-checking or governance
processes.
Instead, ARES is positioned as a **coordination layer**
that orchestrates multiple verification signals into ac-
tionable, auditable decisions under time and uncertainty
constraints.

The breadth of ARES reflects the empirical reality that
modern misinformation campaigns are:
multi-modal ∧coordinated ∧context-dependent ∧time-critical.
(56)
A narrow, single-task system—regardless of state-of-the-
art performance—cannot adequately address such threats
in isolation. Consequently, ARES prioritizes:
• cross-domain consistency,
• graceful degradation under uncertainty,
• explainability and escalation pathways,
• operational deployment feasibility.

In light of the above, claims of “superior performance”
throughout this paper should be interpreted as:
“ARES demonstrates strong, statistically signif-
icant performance across multiple verification
dimensions while maintaining system-level robust-
ness, interpretability, and real-time operability,
rather than optimizing any single task in isola-
tion.”
This framing reflects the system-level goals of ARES and
aligns its evaluation criteria with its intended deployment
context.

XXX. Module-Wise Contribution and
Counterfactual Ablation Analysis
Reported system-level metrics (e.g., F1 = 0.92) summa-
rize end-to-end performance but do not, by themselves,
establish causal contribution of individual modules. To
address this limitation, we perform structured ablation and
counterfactual analysis to quantify how each component
of ARES contributes to the final outcome.
A. ARES as a Compositional System
Let the full ARES system be represented as a composi-
tion of modules:
A = F ◦T ◦B ◦C ◦V ◦E,
(57)
where:
• E: multi-modal encoders (text, image, audio, video),
• V: neural verification models,
• C: symbolic and cross-source logic,
• B: behavioral and bot detection,
• T : temporal claim evolution tracking,
• F: decision fusion and escalation logic.
System-level performance is therefore an emergent prop-
erty of interacting components rather than a monolithic
classifier.

system:
A−X = A \ {X},
where X is removed or replaced with a minimal baseline,
while all remaining modules, datasets, hyperparameters,

importance in isolation. Instead, they quantify contribution

with the system-integration objective of ARES rather than
isolated task optimization.

This ablation and counterfactual analysis establishes

• System-level metrics are decomposable into measur-

• Performance gains persist across multiple independent

• No single component accounts for the majority of

• Causal claims are supported by explicit ARES −X

B. Accessing and Reproducing ARES_POC via GitHub
To ensure full reproducibility of the ARES verification
functional, the complete Proof-of-Concept implementation
is publicly available at:
https://github.com/gurarpitzz/ARES_POC
This repository contains the exact implementation of the
operators described in Section X, including the retrieval
operator R(C), semantic filter S(C, E), entailment operator
N(C, E), source prior W(E), and the verification functional
V (C).
Downloading the Repository: Researchers can obtain the
full source code using either of the following methods:
a) Method 1 — Direct Download (No Git Required):
1) Open the GitHub link.
2) Click the green Code button.
3) Select Download ZIP.
4) Extract the folder locally.
b) Method 2 — Using Git:
git clone https://github.com/gurarpitzz/ARES_POC.git
cd ARES_POC
Installing Dependencies: ARES_POC uses standard
Python libraries listed in requirements.txt. Install them
using:
pip install -r requirements.txt
Running the Verification Engine: ARES can be executed
through the command-line interface:
python main.py "The Earth orbits the Sun" --k 10 --m 5
where:
• k denotes the number of evidence sources retrieved
(R(C)),
• M denotes the number of top semantically similar
passages selected for aggregation (S(C, E)).
Running Benchmark Evaluation:
To reproduce the
benchmark experiments reported in this paper:
python evaluate.py --dataset liar --samples 50
For FEVER evaluation, place the Wikipedia JSONL
dump inside a folder named wiki-pages/ before execution.
Running the Web Interface: ARES_POC also includes
a FastAPI-based interface for interactive visualization:
uvicorn app:app --reload
Then open http://127.0.0.1:8000 in a browser to
observe the mathematical evidence trace in real time.
Repository Structure: The repository is intentionally
organized to directly mirror the mathematical formulation:
• retriever.py →R(C)
• similarity.py →S(C, E)
• entailment.py →N(C, E)
• credibility.py →W(E)
• verifier.py →V (C)
This direct mapping ensures that reviewers can trace
every line of code back to the formal equation defining
ARES.
XXXII. Limitations and Future Work
Despite its robust architecture and multilayered valida-
tion mechanisms, ARES (AI-Driven Real-time Evaluation
System) remains subject to several limitations. This section
discusses known weaknesses and outlines future enhance-
ments aimed at improving accuracy, scalability, and global
applicability.
A. 10.1 Current Limitations
• Low-Resource and Dialectal Language Per-
formance: Accuracy decreases in low-resource or
culturally specific dialects due to limited labeled
misinformation datasets.
• Adversarial Vulnerability: ARES remains sensitive
to adversarial attacks such as synonym substitutions,
homoglyph obfuscation (e.g., replacing o with 0), or
dataset poisoning.
• Latency at Extreme Scale: Multi-stage verification
(symbolic inference + transformer + FAISS matching)
may introduce noticeable latency in high-volume surge
periods.
• Insufficient Cultural Contextualization: Irony,
sarcasm, satire, and culturally symbolic references
may be misclassified without contextual grounding.
• Limited Human-in-the-Loop for Edge Cases:
While high-confidence predictions are reliable, socially
sensitive borderline cases would benefit from immedi-
ate human review.

• skewed training data distributions,

ARES integrates multiple external dependencies, in-
cluding OSINT feeds and structured knowledge bases.
Let K = {K1, K2, . . . , Kn} denote these sources. System
reliability assumes partial correctness and availability of

Failure modes include:
• outdated or incomplete knowledge bases,
• coordinated poisoning or manipulation of open-source
data,
• temporary unavailability of external APIs.

and fallback logic; however, adversarial manipulation of
multiple correlated sources remains a known limitation.
D. Regional and Linguistic Asymmetries
Performance across regions and languages is inherently
uneven due to disparities in:
• training data volume,
• quality of available fact-checking sources,
• geopolitical context coverage.
Empirically, ARES exhibits higher confidence calibration
in high-resource languages and regions with dense OSINT
coverage. In contrast, low-resource or rapidly evolving
regional contexts may experience:
• increased uncertainty classifications,
• higher escalation rates,

E. Human-in-the-Loop Subjectivity
Although human analyst intervention improves safety
and adaptability, it introduces variability due to subjective
judgment, analyst expertise, and contextual interpretation.
While consensus protocols and audit logs reduce inconsis-

This trade-off is intrinsic to any hybrid AI–human

F. Summary of Limitations
In summary, ARES is constrained by:
• residual bias inherited from data and knowledge
sources,
• dependency on external OSINT reliability,
• uneven performance across regions and languages,
• inherent subjectivity in human oversight.
These limitations do not negate the system’s contribu-

ARES is intended to function.

• Crowd-Sourced Verification Layer: Verified fact-

contested claims in real time, supported by reputation-
weighted consensus mechanisms.

Fine-tuning on low-resource linguistic corpora and

systems, and government misinformation alert sys-
